hero.kicker: Full stack engineer · Austin, TX · open to remote
headline: I build the whole site,
from the React component
to the server behind it.
hero.lede: Full stack software engineer at GoDaddy. About half my work is React and TypeScript, half is the server-rendered Node.js layer behind them, on a site that serves three brands. I also built the GitHub Actions automation that ships it.

platform.heading: Content goes in one end. A multi-brand website comes out the other.
body: Editors author structured content in Contentful. It gets transformed and mapped onto a shared React and TypeScript component library, rendered server-side, and served as the customer-facing site across GoDaddy, Afternic, and 123 Reg — with routing, navigation, search, brand configuration, and internationalization all resolved along the way.

I work across that whole chain, about half on the frontend and half on the server: the Node.js transforms and service integrations, the component interfaces, the rendering behavior, and the CDN delivery that puts it in front of people. In my first year I built and unit-tested features in the .NET Core (C#) services behind the site.

cards.title: Internationalization
cards.body: Right-to-left layout and translation handling inside components that several brand experiences consume. A shared component can't assume the direction text runs.

cards.title: React 18 → 19
cards.body: Contributed to moving the shared platform onto React 19 — working the breaking changes across the component library and the applications that consume it, without a flag day for the teams downstream.

cards.title: Content-to-component alignment
cards.body: Contributed to keeping component interfaces aligned with Contentful content schemas, so a content-model change and the component that renders it don't drift apart silently.

lead.heading: I also own how it ships.
lead.sub: The shared library publishes several times a day and the site consumes it about as often. Here is what that used to cost, and the GitHub Actions automation I built to stop paying it.
lead.note: My manager and our technical program manager point people at me as the team's subject-matter expert for developer experience and CI/CD.

machine.heading: Every release used to be walked across four repositories by hand.
machine.sub: So I built the thing that walks it. Press play.

outcomes.title: Deploys stopped batching
outcomes.body: Teams had been deferring releases rather than hand-trace package ownership. Removing the handoff removed the reason to wait. Early adoption merged 14+ automated bumps.

outcomes.title: A defect class closed
outcomes.body: Shared-package versions used to ship decoupled from the changes they belonged to. Reconciliation makes that state unrepresentable.

outcomes.title: The merge stayed human
outcomes.body: Deliberately. The system generates a validated draft PR and stops.

projects.title: My first year: .NET Core services
projects.body: I was hired to write React and placed on the team that owned the site's .NET Core (C#) services, because that is where the need was. I learned C# on the job and spent the year building and unit-testing features in those services.

projects.title: A domain page that drives $1M+ a year
projects.body: I rebuilt a gTLD domain product page that drives more than $1M a year in revenue, moved the domain experiences from class components to hooks, and extended the TLD-availability and domain-purchase integrations behind them.

projects.title: One component, many brands
projects.body: Theme and intent abstractions that separate behavior and semantics from brand presentation, so shared React infrastructure serves several brand experiences without forking a component per brand.

projects.title: CMS to components, server-side
projects.body: I contributed to the Sitecore to Contentful modernization on the shared rendering layer: content transforms, a facade and component map, and shared packages that behave the same on the server as in the browser — no assumed window, no hydration surprises.

projects.title: Sticky-stack: independent roots, one stack
projects.body: The CMS could render three sticky navigation elements as separate React roots, so top: 0 made them collide — no shared parent owned the layout. I built a portal-based stacking surface with a registry, deterministic ordering and measured dynamic offsets, exposed to product teams as a single hook.

projects.title: Merge queues that actually validate
projects.body: A merge queue evaluates a temporary merge-group state, not the PR head — so required checks have to understand that path or they are validating the wrong thing. I made merge-group validation correct first, then cut waste: selective execution, cancelling superseded runs, and reusing cached build output.

about.heading: I learned the stack by going where the work was
about.sub: I was hired to write React. The first real need was on the team that owned the site's .NET Core services, so I spent my first year learning C# there. Since then I've worked across the whole site: components, the server layer, the integrations, and the pipeline that ships it.
more: What ties it together is leverage. A feature ships once; a shared component, a service integration or a release workflow gets used for years. It's also why I wrote and taught a four-hour React bootcamp for interns.

I'm also careful about what I claim. If I tell you a system saved time, I'll tell you how I'd measure it — and where I haven't yet. That habit has made me better at engineering than any framework has.
